summary: Ovarian and adnexal masses range from harmless functional cysts to PCOS, a whole-body endocrine and metabolic disorder. Exams test which cyst fits the clinical setting, why an enlarged ovary twists, and how insulin resistance and LH drive androgen excess in PCOS.

points: Follicular cyst: a follicle that fails to rupture keeps growing; the most common functional cyst, usually resolves in a few cycles.
Follicular cysts can keep making estrogen, which may cause irregular bleeding and, rarely, endometrial hyperplasia or precocious puberty in girls.
Corpus luteum cyst: forms after ovulation; bleeding into it can rupture into the peritoneum, giving sudden pain and hemoperitoneum that can mimic ectopic pregnancy.
Theca lutein cysts: usually bilateral and multiple; very high hCG overstimulates theca cells (hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma, multiple gestation, ovarian hyperstimulation).
Theca lutein cysts regress once hCG falls, such as after a mole is evacuated.
The ovary twists on the infundibulopelvic (suspensory) ligament and the utero-ovarian ligament, which carry its blood supply.
Usually needs an enlarged ovary as a lever: a cyst, teratoma, or other mass, often larger than about 5 cm.
Thin-walled veins and lymphatics close first, so the ovary swells with edema and congestion; rising pressure then blocks arterial inflow and the ovary infarcts.
Presents with sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain, nausea, and vomiting; Doppler may show absent flow, though normal flow does not rule torsion out.
Thin-walled cysts in the broad ligament (mesosalpinx) between the tube and ovary, arising from Wolffian (mesonephric) or Mullerian (paramesonephric) remnants or mesothelium.
Imaging shows a separate, normal ovary beside the cyst, which helps set it apart from an ovarian cyst.
Mostly asymptomatic and benign; large ones can twist, bleed, or rupture.
Faster GnRH pulses favor LH over FSH, so the LH to FSH ratio rises (often above 2 to 1).
LH drives theca cells to make androgens; relatively low FSH means granulosa aromatase cannot convert them all to estradiol.
Insulin resistance gives high insulin, which acts with LH on theca cells to raise androgen output and lowers hepatic SHBG, so free testosterone rises.
Excess androgen arrests follicle development, leaving many small follicles along the cortex (string of pearls) and no ovulation.
Adipose tissue aromatizes androgens to estrone, giving steady estrogen with no progesterone (unopposed estrogen).
Rotterdam criteria (2 of 3): oligo or anovulation, clinical or lab hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound.
Findings: oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea, hirsutism, acne, male-pattern hair thinning, obesity, acanthosis nigricans.
Complications: infertility, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, fatty liver, obstructive sleep apnea, and endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma from unopposed estrogen.
A complication of PID: ascending infection (often begun by N. gonorrhoeae or C. trachomatis, then mixed with anaerobes) inflames the tube, which adheres to the ovary.
The result is a fluid-filled or pus-filled tubo-ovarian complex: fever, pelvic pain, adnexal mass, and cervical motion tenderness.
Rupture spills pus into the peritoneum, causing peritonitis and sepsis.
Scarring later causes infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain, and hydrosalpinx.

tricks.label: Name the cyst by the hormone around it
tricks.text: Before ovulation, the follicular cyst can make estrogen. After ovulation, the corpus luteum cyst bleeds. Very high hCG gives theca lutein cysts on both sides.

tricks.label: Torsion follows the veins first
tricks.text: Veins collapse before arteries because their walls are thin and their pressure is low. So the twisted ovary swells first, then infarcts.

tricks.label: PCOS in one loop
tricks.text: Insulin and LH push theca cells to make androgen, androgen stops follicles, no ovulation means no progesterone, and estrogen goes unopposed on the endometrium.

highYield: Bilateral theca lutein cysts point to very high hCG, especially a complete hydatidiform mole.
A ruptured corpus luteum cyst can cause hemoperitoneum and mimic ruptured ectopic pregnancy.
Ovarian torsion needs an enlarged ovary; mature cystic teratoma is a classic lead point.
PCOS: LH to FSH ratio high, insulin resistance lowers SHBG, free testosterone rises.
PCOS raises the risk of endometrial carcinoma through chronic unopposed estrogen.
Acanthosis nigricans in a woman with irregular cycles signals insulin resistance and PCOS.
Tubo-ovarian abscess is a complication of PID and can rupture into the peritoneum.
pitfalls: Paraovarian versus ovarian cyst: a paraovarian cyst sits in the broad ligament with a normal ovary seen separately.
Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound alone do not make PCOS; Rotterdam needs two of three criteria.
Theca lutein cysts are bilateral and hCG-driven; follicular and corpus luteum cysts are usually single.
Normal Doppler flow does not exclude torsion, because the arterial supply can be partly preserved early.
Tubo-ovarian abscess is an infection with fever and leukocytosis; a hemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst gives sudden pain without fever.

dumps.p: Draw a theca cell and a granulosa cell side by side. Show how LH, FSH, and insulin act on them, then trace the effects to the liver, fat, and endometrium.
l: Fast GnRH pulses raise LH relative to FSH
LH stimulates theca cells to make androgens
Low FSH limits granulosa aromatase, so less estradiol
Insulin adds to theca androgen output
Insulin lowers hepatic SHBG, raising free testosterone
Androgen excess arrests follicles, giving anovulation and many small follicles
Fat aromatizes androgen to estrone, giving unopposed estrogen
Unopposed estrogen leads to endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma

dumps.p: On blank paper, build a table with rows for follicular cyst, corpus luteum cyst, theca lutein cysts, paraovarian cyst, and tubo-ovarian abscess. Columns: origin, one side or both, hormone link, main complication.
l: Follicular: unruptured follicle, usually one side, may make estrogen
Corpus luteum: after ovulation, one side, bleeds and may cause hemoperitoneum
Theca lutein: both sides, driven by high hCG (mole, multiple gestation)
Paraovarian: broad ligament remnant, separate normal ovary
Tubo-ovarian abscess: PID complication with fever and adnexal mass
Any enlarged adnexal mass can twist (torsion)
Tubo-ovarian abscess can rupture and cause peritonitis

summary: Placental disease covers gestational trophoblastic disease (moles and choriocarcinoma), preeclampsia, and problems of placental position, attachment, and amniotic fluid. Exams test the genetics of moles, the vascular story of preeclampsia, and how to tell painful from painless third-trimester bleeding.

points: Complete mole: an empty ovum (no maternal DNA) is fertilized by one sperm that duplicates, giving 46,XX; less often two sperm give 46,XY.
All DNA is paternal, so p57 (a maternally expressed gene) is negative; no fetal parts; all villi swell; trophoblast proliferates diffusely.
Partial mole: one normal ovum plus two sperm gives a triploid karyotype (69,XXY most often); fetal parts present, focal villous swelling, p57 positive.
Complete moles carry the higher risk of invasive mole and choriocarcinoma (choriocarcinoma about 2 to 3 percent); partial moles rarely progress.
Vaginal bleeding in the first half of pregnancy, uterus large for dates, no fetal heart tones.
Very high hCG causes hyperemesis gravidarum and bilateral theca lutein cysts.
hCG shares its alpha subunit with TSH and weakly stimulates the TSH receptor, so hyperthyroidism can occur.
Preeclampsia before 20 weeks of gestation strongly suggests a mole.
Ultrasound shows a snowstorm or cluster-of-grapes pattern; after evacuation, serial hCG must fall to zero.
Invasive mole: hydropic villi grow into the myometrium; it can perforate the uterus and bleed; hCG stays high after evacuation.
Gestational choriocarcinoma: malignant cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast with no villi, forming a hemorrhagic, necrotic mass.
About half arise after a complete mole; the rest follow abortion, normal pregnancy, or ectopic pregnancy.
hCG is very high; spread is early and through the blood, to lung (cough, hemoptysis), vagina, brain, and liver.
Gestational choriocarcinoma responds very well to chemotherapy.
Cytotrophoblast fails to remodel the spiral arteries, so they stay narrow, muscular, and high-resistance; the placenta becomes ischemic.
The ischemic placenta releases sFlt-1 (binds VEGF and PlGF) and soluble endoglin (binds TGF-beta), causing maternal endothelial dysfunction.
Less nitric oxide and prostacyclin, more thromboxane: vasospasm, hypertension, leaky vessels, and glomerular endotheliosis with proteinuria.

Definition: new blood pressure of 140/90 mm Hg or higher after 20 weeks, with proteinuria or end-organ damage (low platelets, high creatinine, high transaminases, pulmonary edema, headache, visual change).
Risk factors: nulliparity, prior preeclampsia, chronic hypertension, diabetes, kidney disease, antiphospholipid syndrome, obesity, multiple gestation, molar pregnancy.
Complications: eclampsia (seizures), HELLP syndrome, placental abruption, fetal growth restriction, stroke, DIC, liver rupture.
Placental abruption: the placenta separates early; painful bleeding, tender firm uterus, fetal distress; the released tissue factor can trigger DIC.
Abruption risks: hypertension and preeclampsia, cocaine, smoking, abdominal trauma, prior abruption.
Placenta previa: placenta covers or lies near the internal cervical os; painless bright red bleeding in the third trimester.
Placenta accreta spectrum: villi attach to (accreta), invade into (increta), or go through (percreta) the myometrium because the decidua basalis is deficient.
Biggest accreta risks are prior cesarean delivery and placenta previa together; the placenta does not separate, causing severe postpartum hemorrhage.
After about 16 weeks, fetal urine makes most of the amniotic fluid, and fetal swallowing removes it.
Oligohydramnios: too little urine (bilateral renal agenesis, posterior urethral valves, placental insufficiency) or ruptured membranes.
Potter sequence: low fluid compresses the fetus, giving pulmonary hypoplasia, flat face, limb deformities such as clubfeet.
Polyhydramnios: poor swallowing (esophageal or duodenal atresia, anencephaly) or maternal diabetes (fetal hyperglycemia causes osmotic diuresis).

tricks.label: Complete is all dad
tricks.text: A complete mole has only paternal DNA, so the maternally expressed p57 is missing and no fetus forms. A partial mole has mom's set too, so p57 is present and fetal parts appear.

tricks.label: Preeclampsia clock
tricks.text: Hypertension with proteinuria after 20 weeks is preeclampsia. The same picture before 20 weeks should make you think of a hydatidiform mole.

tricks.label: Pain sorts the bleed
tricks.text: Abruption hurts because blood dissects behind the placenta and irritates the uterus. Previa bleeds painlessly because the placenta simply tears from a stretching lower segment.

tricks.label: Fluid in, fluid out
tricks.text: The fetus makes amniotic fluid as urine and removes it by swallowing. Kidney or urinary problems give too little fluid; swallowing problems give too much.

highYield: Complete mole is 46,XX with all-paternal DNA, no fetal parts, and negative p57.
Very high hCG explains hyperemesis, theca lutein cysts, and hyperthyroidism in a molar pregnancy.
Persistent or rising hCG after mole evacuation means invasive mole or choriocarcinoma.
Choriocarcinoma has no villi and spreads early through the blood, most often to the lung.
Preeclampsia starts with failed spiral artery remodeling and antiangiogenic sFlt-1 release.
HELLP: hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets.
Painful bleeding is abruption; painless bleeding is previa; prior cesarean plus previa predicts accreta.
Bilateral renal agenesis gives oligohydramnios and Potter sequence with fatal pulmonary hypoplasia.
pitfalls: Partial mole is triploid and has fetal parts; complete mole is diploid and has none.
Invasive mole keeps its villi; choriocarcinoma has no villi at all.
Choriocarcinoma can follow a normal pregnancy, so a high hCG with lung nodules months after delivery should raise it.
Eclampsia means preeclampsia plus seizures; seizures from another cause are a different diagnosis.
Accreta is about depth of attachment; previa is about location over the os, though the two often occur together.

Preeclampsia: remodeling fails, vessels stay narrow, placenta becomes ischemic

summary: This unit covers the Bartholin cyst and pelvic organ prolapse (cystocele, urethrocele, rectocele). Exams test where each lesion sits, what weakens the pelvic floor, and which symptom points to which organ.

points: Bartholin (greater vestibular) glands lie posterolateral to the vaginal opening, at about the 4 and 8 o'clock positions; they lubricate the vestibule.
Blockage of the duct (from inflammation, trauma, or thick mucus) traps secretions and forms a cyst in the posterolateral vestibule.
Infection turns it into an abscess: a hot, tender, fluctuant swelling that makes sitting and walking painful.
Mostly in reproductive-age women; a new Bartholin mass after about age 40 needs biopsy to exclude carcinoma.
The male homolog is the bulbourethral (Cowper) gland.
Support comes from the levator ani, the endopelvic fascia (pubocervical anteriorly, rectovaginal posteriorly), and the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments.
Vaginal childbirth stretches and tears the levator ani and fascia and can injure the pudendal nerve.
Other risks: aging, estrogen loss after menopause, obesity, chronic cough, chronic constipation and straining, heavy lifting, connective tissue disorders.
Prolapse feels like pelvic pressure or a bulge at the vaginal opening that worsens with standing or straining.
Cystocele: the bladder bulges into the upper anterior vaginal wall through a weak pubocervical fascia.
Cystocele symptoms: incomplete emptying, frequency, urinary retention, recurrent UTIs; some women press the bulge to void.
Urethrocele: the urethra bulges into the distal anterior wall; a mobile urethra loses support and leaks with cough or laughter (stress incontinence).
Rectocele: the rectum bulges into the posterior vaginal wall through a weak rectovaginal septum.
Rectocele symptoms: hard-to-pass stools, incomplete evacuation, pressing on the posterior vaginal wall or perineum to defecate.

tricks.label: Front is urine, back is stool
tricks.text: Anterior wall bulges (cystocele, urethrocele) cause urinary symptoms. Posterior wall bulges (rectocele) cause trouble with bowel movements.

tricks.label: Upper versus lower front wall
tricks.text: The bladder sits higher, so a cystocele bulges the upper anterior wall and causes retention. The urethra sits lower, so a urethrocele bulges the distal anterior wall and causes stress leakage.

highYield: Bartholin cyst sits in the posterolateral vestibule at about 4 or 8 o'clock.
A Bartholin mass in a woman over about 40 is biopsied to rule out carcinoma.
Vaginal childbirth is the main risk factor for pelvic organ prolapse.
Estrogen loss after menopause weakens pelvic connective tissue and adds to prolapse.
Cystocele causes incomplete bladder emptying and recurrent UTIs.
Urethrocele causes stress incontinence; rectocele causes difficult defecation.
pitfalls: Bartholin cyst sits posterolateral at the vestibule; a Skene gland cyst sits beside the urethral opening.
The vaginal wall that bulges tells cystocele from rectocele: anterior is bladder, posterior is rectum.
Stress incontinence (leak with cough) points to urethral hypermobility; urge incontinence comes from detrusor overactivity.
Enterocele (small bowel in the upper posterior vagina) can mimic a high rectocele.

dumps.p: Draw a midline sagittal view of the female pelvis. Label bladder, urethra, vagina, uterus, rectum, and levator ani, then draw where a cystocele, urethrocele, and rectocele bulge and write one symptom for each.

Levator ani forms the floor; endopelvic fascia supports the walls
Cystocele: bladder into upper anterior wall
Cystocele symptom: incomplete emptying or recurrent UTI
Urethrocele: urethra into distal anterior wall, stress incontinence
Rectocele: rectum into posterior wall, difficult defecation
Main risks: vaginal childbirth, aging, menopause, obesity, chronic straining

summary: This unit gathers the precancers and tumors of the cervix, uterus, ovary, vagina, vulva, prostate, penis, and testis. Exams test the driver of each tumor (HPV, estrogen, germline mutations), the cell of origin, the tumor marker, and the typical spread.

points: High-risk HPV (16, 18) infects the transformation zone; E6 degrades p53, E7 inactivates RB, and koilocytes (raisin-like nucleus, clear perinuclear halo) mark infection.
CIN grade = how much epithelium atypical immature cells replace: CIN 1 lower third (LSIL), CIN 2 lower two-thirds, CIN 3 more than two-thirds to full thickness (CIN 2 and 3 are HSIL).
Risks: persistent HPV 16 or 18, early first intercourse, many partners, smoking, HIV and other immunodeficiency; most CIN 1 regresses.
Invasive cervical carcinoma is mostly squamous, with some adenocarcinoma; it presents with postcoital or irregular bleeding.
Lateral spread into the parametrium blocks the ureters, causing hydronephrosis and renal failure, a common cause of death.
Unopposed estrogen causes hyperplasia: obesity, anovulation, PCOS, estrogen-only therapy, granulosa cell tumor; PTEN loss is common.
Atypical hyperplasia is the direct precursor of endometrioid carcinoma.
Endometrioid carcinoma: perimenopausal, estrogen-related, arises from hyperplasia; PTEN mutations and mismatch repair defects (Lynch syndrome).
Serous carcinoma: older women, atrophic endometrium, TP53 mutation, spreads early through the peritoneum, poor prognosis; both types present with postmenopausal bleeding.
Endometrial and endocervical polyps: benign overgrowths of glands and stroma causing intermenstrual or abnormal bleeding.

Leiomyoma (fibroid): most common benign tumor in women; estrogen-sensitive smooth muscle, well circumscribed, whorled; often multiple; more common in Black women; grows in pregnancy, shrinks after menopause.
Fibroids cause heavy bleeding with iron deficiency anemia, pelvic pressure, and infertility (submucosal type).
Leiomyosarcoma: arises on its own in older women as a single large soft mass with necrosis, atypia, and many mitoses; leiomyomas do not transform into it.
Surface epithelial tumors (serous, mucinous, endometrioid, clear cell, Brenner) make up most ovarian tumors and most ovarian cancers.
High-grade serous carcinoma: TP53 in nearly all, BRCA1 or BRCA2 in many; often begins in the fallopian tube fimbria.
Serous carcinoma shows psammoma bodies, raised CA-125, ascites, and peritoneal and omental spread.
Germ cell: mature cystic teratoma (most common), struma ovarii (thyroid tissue, can cause hyperthyroidism), dysgerminoma (clear cells, LDH), yolk sac tumor (Schiller-Duval bodies, AFP).
Sex cord-stromal: granulosa cell tumor (estrogen, Call-Exner bodies), Sertoli-Leydig (androgen, virilization), fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion (Meigs syndrome).
Krukenberg tumor: bilateral ovarian metastasis of mucin-filled signet ring cells, usually from the stomach.
Adenocarcinoma risks: age, Black race, family history, BRCA2.
Arises in the peripheral (posterior) zone, so it can be felt on rectal exam and rarely causes early urinary obstruction.
Gleason score adds the two most common gland patterns (each graded 1 to 5); PSA rises, though BPH and prostatitis raise it too.
Spreads through the vertebral venous plexus to the lumbar spine and pelvis, making osteoblastic metastases with bone pain and raised alkaline phosphatase.
Penile squamous cell carcinoma: HPV 16, uncircumcised penis, phimosis, smoking; in situ forms are Bowen disease, erythroplasia of Queyrat, and bowenoid papulosis.

Testicular tumors: most are germ cell, with isochromosome 12p and germ cell neoplasia in situ as precursor; painless firm mass that does not transilluminate; risks are cryptorchidism, Klinefelter syndrome, gonadal dysgenesis, and a prior testicular tumor.
Seminoma: most common, uniform clear cells with lymphocytes, placental alkaline phosphatase, very radiosensitive, good prognosis; AFP stays normal.
Yolk sac tumor raises AFP; choriocarcinoma raises hCG; embryonal carcinoma is aggressive and hemorrhagic.
Leydig cell tumor: Reinke crystals; androgen causes precocious puberty in boys, estrogen causes gynecomastia in men.
Lymphoma is the most common testicular tumor in men over 60.
Vaginal squamous cell carcinoma: older women, HPV, arises from vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia.
Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina: young women exposed to DES in utero.
Sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma): grape-like vaginal mass in girls under about 5, desmin positive.
HPV-related vulvar carcinoma: younger women, arises from usual (HPV-related) VIN.
HPV-independent vulvar carcinoma: older women with lichen sclerosus, arises from differentiated VIN with TP53 mutation.
Extramammary Paget disease of the vulva: intraepithelial adenocarcinoma cells in the epidermis, usually with no underlying carcinoma, unlike Paget disease of the breast.

tricks.label: E6 with p53, E7 with RB
tricks.text: Pair them in order: the lower number, E6, takes the suppressor with a number in its name (p53); E7 takes RB. Losing both brakes lets infected cells divide and pile up mutations.

tricks.label: Two endometrial cancers, two backgrounds
tricks.text: Endometrioid grows on a background of too much estrogen (hyperplasia, younger, obese). Serous grows on a thin, atrophic endometrium in an older woman, carries TP53, and spreads fast.

tricks.label: Markers by tissue
tricks.text: Yolk sac makes AFP the way fetal yolk sac does. Trophoblast makes hCG the way placenta does. Seminoma and dysgerminoma are twins: clear cells, lymphocytes, normal AFP.

tricks.label: Testis drains to the abdomen
tricks.text: The testis descends from the posterior abdominal wall, so its lymph goes to para-aortic nodes. The scrotal skin drains to superficial inguinal nodes.

highYield: Cervical carcinoma kills through ureteral obstruction and renal failure.
Atypical endometrial hyperplasia is the precursor of endometrioid carcinoma; serous carcinoma carries TP53 and arises in atrophic endometrium.
Leiomyomas do not become leiomyosarcomas.
Prostate cancer arises in the peripheral zone and sends osteoblastic metastases to the lumbar spine through the vertebral venous plexus.
High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma: TP53, BRCA1 or BRCA2, tubal origin, CA-125, psammoma bodies.
Granulosa cell tumor makes estrogen (Call-Exner bodies); Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor virilizes.
Seminoma has placental alkaline phosphatase and normal AFP; yolk sac tumor raises AFP; choriocarcinoma raises hCG.
In utero DES exposure leads to clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina.
pitfalls: Extramammary Paget disease of the vulva usually has no underlying carcinoma; Paget disease of the breast nearly always does.
Benign prostatic hyperplasia arises in the transition zone; prostate carcinoma arises in the peripheral zone.
Krukenberg tumor is bilateral metastatic signet ring carcinoma; a primary mucinous ovarian tumor is usually one-sided.
Testicular masses that transilluminate are fluid (hydrocele, spermatocele); a solid tumor does not.
Struma ovarii causes hyperthyroidism from ovarian thyroid tissue, while a mole causes it through hCG.

dumps.p: On blank paper, draw a tree with three branches: surface epithelial, germ cell, and sex cord-stromal. Put each ovarian tumor on its branch with one key feature and its marker or hormone, then add Krukenberg tumor off to the side.
l: Surface epithelial: serous (psammoma bodies, CA-125), mucinous, endometrioid, clear cell, Brenner
High-grade serous: TP53, BRCA1 or BRCA2, begins in the tubal fimbria
Germ cell: mature cystic teratoma (most common), struma ovarii (hyperthyroidism)
Dysgerminoma: clear cells, LDH; yolk sac tumor: Schiller-Duval bodies, AFP
Granulosa cell: estrogen, Call-Exner bodies, endometrial hyperplasia
Sertoli-Leydig: androgen, virilization
Fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion is Meigs syndrome
Krukenberg: bilateral signet ring metastasis, usually gastric

dumps.p: Draw the cervix with its transformation zone. Trace how high-risk HPV leads from infection to CIN 1, CIN 2, CIN 3, and invasive carcinoma, and show how lateral spread harms the kidneys.
l: Transformation zone is where columnar cells undergo squamous metaplasia
High-risk HPV 16 and 18 infect immature metaplastic cells
E6 degrades p53; E7 inactivates RB
Koilocytes mark HPV infection
CIN 1 lower third (LSIL); CIN 2 and 3 thicker (HSIL)
Most CIN 1 regresses; persistent high-risk HPV drives progression
Invasive carcinoma is mostly squamous; presents with postcoital bleeding
Parametrial spread blocks ureters: hydronephrosis and renal failure

summary: Genitourinary infections include the classic sexually transmitted infections, bacterial vaginosis, and toxic shock syndrome. Exams test the organism behind each ulcer or discharge, the bedside tests that separate the vaginitides, syphilis serology, and the late or neonatal complications.

points: Primary syphilis (Treponema pallidum): single painless indurated chancre with a clean base and painless rubbery nodes.
Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi, gram-negative coccobacillus): painful soft ulcer with ragged undermined edges and gray-yellow exudate; painful inguinal nodes that may suppurate.
Genital herpes (HSV-2 mostly, HSV-1 rising): painful grouped vesicles on a red base that break into shallow ulcers.
Primary herpes adds fever, malaise, tender nodes, and dysuria; the virus then hides in sacral sensory ganglia and reactivates as milder outbreaks.
Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells; neonatal herpes is mostly acquired during vaginal delivery.
Lymphogranuloma venereum (C. trachomatis L1 to L3): small painless ulcer, then painful inguinal buboes; can cause proctocolitis and strictures.
Normal vaginal pH is about 3.8 to 4.5, kept low by lactic acid from lactobacilli.
Bacterial vaginosis: lactobacilli are replaced by Gardnerella vaginalis and anaerobes; thin gray fishy discharge, pH above 4.5, positive whiff test, clue cells, few neutrophils.
Trichomoniasis: flagellated protozoan; frothy yellow-green malodorous discharge, strawberry cervix, pH above 4.5, motile trophozoites and many neutrophils on wet mount.
Candidal vaginitis: thick white curdy discharge, itching, pH normal, negative whiff test, pseudohyphae on KOH prep.
C. trachomatis (serovars D to K) is obligate intracellular: infectious elementary body outside the cell, replicating reticulate body inside.
Chlamydia is often silent; it causes urethritis, cervicitis, epididymitis, PID, and reactive arthritis.
Neonatal chlamydia: conjunctivitis at about 1 to 2 weeks, then afebrile staccato-cough pneumonia at 1 to 3 months.
N. gonorrhoeae: purulent urethral discharge with intracellular gram-negative diplococci in neutrophils; cervicitis, PID, and neonatal conjunctivitis in the first few days.
Disseminated gonococcal infection: septic arthritis (often the knee), or tenosynovitis with pustular skin lesions and polyarthralgia.
Pili undergo antigenic variation, so reinfection is common; C5 to C9 (membrane attack complex) deficiency causes recurrent Neisseria infection.
HPV 6 and 11 cause condylomata acuminata: soft cauliflower-like warts with koilocytes.
Condylomata lata of secondary syphilis are flat, moist, gray plaques full of spirochetes.
High-risk HPV (16, 18) causes cervical, vulvar, vaginal, penile, anal, and oropharyngeal carcinoma.
Nongonococcal urethritis: C. trachomatis most often, then Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma urealyticum, and Trichomonas vaginalis.
Reactive arthritis after urethritis (or enteric infection): arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis, mostly in HLA-B27-positive men.
Primary: painless chancre about 3 weeks after exposure; heals on its own.
Secondary: rash on trunk, palms, and soles, condylomata lata, generalized lymphadenopathy, fever, patchy hair loss.
Latent: no signs, positive serology. Tertiary (years later): gummas, aortitis of the ascending aorta (vasa vasorum endarteritis, aneurysm, aortic regurgitation), tabes dorsalis.
Tabes dorsalis damages dorsal columns and roots: lost proprioception, positive Romberg sign, shooting pains, Argyll Robertson pupils.
Nontreponemal tests (VDRL, RPR) detect anticardiolipin antibody; titers track activity and fall with treatment; false positives in pregnancy, SLE, viral infections.
Treponemal tests (FTA-ABS) detect antibody to the organism and stay positive for life, so they confirm infection without showing activity.
Congenital syphilis: snuffles, rash, saddle nose, Hutchinson teeth, mulberry molars, saber shins, sensorineural deafness.
S. aureus makes TSST-1, a superantigen that links MHC class II to the T cell receptor Vbeta region outside the peptide groove.
Up to about 20 percent of T cells fire at once, releasing IL-2, IFN-gamma, IL-1, and TNF in a cytokine storm.
Settings: retained or superabsorbent tampons, nasal packing, surgical wounds, postpartum infection.
Findings: fever of 38.9 °C (102 °F) or higher, hypotension, diffuse sunburn-like rash, desquamation of palms and soles 1 to 2 weeks later, and injury to three or more organ systems.

tricks.label: You do cry with ducreyi
tricks.text: Chancroid from Haemophilus ducreyi is the painful ulcer; the syphilis chancre is painless.

tricks.label: VDRL false positives: VDRL
tricks.text: Viral infection (mononucleosis, hepatitis), Drugs (injection drug use), Rheumatic fever and rheumatoid arthritis, Lupus and leprosy. Pregnancy also gives false positives.

tricks.label: Can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree
tricks.text: Reactive arthritis: conjunctivitis, urethritis, and arthritis, often after chlamydia in HLA-B27-positive men.

tricks.label: Acuminata versus lata
tricks.text: Acuminata means pointed: raised cauliflower HPV warts. Lata means broad: flat, moist plaques of secondary syphilis that are full of spirochetes.

highYield: Painful ulcer with painful suppurative nodes is chancroid; painless indurated ulcer is syphilis.
Clue cells and a positive whiff test with few neutrophils mean bacterial vaginosis.
Recurrent Neisseria infections point to terminal complement (C5 to C9) deficiency.
Chlamydia is the most common cause of nongonococcal urethritis and is often silent in women.
Tertiary syphilis aortitis hits the ascending aorta through endarteritis of the vasa vasorum.
FTA-ABS stays positive for life; RPR or VDRL titer follows treatment response.
TSST-1 is a superantigen that bypasses normal antigen processing and activates many T cells at once.
Hutchinson teeth, saddle nose, and saber shins mark late congenital syphilis.
pitfalls: Trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis both raise pH above 4.5; neutrophils and motile organisms point to trichomonas, clue cells to BV.
LGV ulcer is painless and small; the painful part is the later inguinal buboes.
Gonococcal neonatal conjunctivitis starts in the first few days; chlamydial conjunctivitis starts at about 1 to 2 weeks.
A positive RPR with negative FTA-ABS suggests a false positive, as in pregnancy or SLE.
Menstrual toxic shock from S. aureus usually has negative blood cultures, because the disease comes from toxin.

dumps.p: Draw a timeline from exposure to tertiary syphilis. Mark each stage with its findings, then add a box comparing nontreponemal and treponemal tests and a list of congenital syphilis findings.
l: Primary: painless indurated chancre about 3 weeks after exposure
Secondary: palm and sole rash, condylomata lata, lymphadenopathy
Latent: no signs, positive serology
Tertiary: gummas, ascending aortitis, tabes dorsalis, Argyll Robertson pupils
VDRL and RPR: anticardiolipin, titer tracks activity, false positives
FTA-ABS: specific, stays positive for life
Congenital: snuffles, Hutchinson teeth, mulberry molars, saddle nose, saber shins, deafness

l: BV: thin gray fishy, pH above 4.5, whiff positive, clue cells
Trichomonas: frothy green, pH above 4.5, motile trophozoites, strawberry cervix
Candida: thick white, normal pH, whiff negative, pseudohyphae
Syphilis: T. pallidum, painless indurated chancre, painless nodes
Chancroid: H. ducreyi, painful ragged ulcer, painful suppurative nodes
Herpes: HSV-2, painful grouped vesicles, tender nodes
LGV: C. trachomatis L1 to L3, painless small ulcer, then painful buboes
